Title: Parametric optimization of the slot waveguide characteristics using a machine-learning approach
Text:
Parametric optimization of the slot 
waveguide characteristics using a 
machine-learning approach
Yadvendra Singh1, Suraj Jena2 & Harish Subbaraman1
Slot waveguides provide high electric field amplitude and optical power in low-index materials that 
are not possible with conventional waveguides. This specific property of the slot waveguide provides 
interaction between active material and electric field, which led to many interesting applications, 
such as optical amplification, optical switching, and optical detection in integrated photonics. In the 
present work, we combine machine learning (ML) algorithms and finite element simulation to predict 
the power confinement (Pconf) and mode effective index (neff) of slot waveguides with respect to 
geometric parameters such as gap, slab width, and slab height. Three different ML techniques, such as 
artificial neural network (ANN), support vector regression (SVR), and random forest (RF), were tested 
to compute performance parameters for the slot waveguide. The RF method outperformed the other 
two with mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), coefficient of determination 
(R2), and Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values corresponding neff and Pconf as 0.007, 0.054, 0.961, 
and 0.960, and 0.129, 0.185, 0.998, and 0.998, respectively. Thus, providing a useful ML methodology 
for efficient optimization of slot waveguide structures for future applications.
A slot waveguide is an advanced optical waveguide structure consisting of a narrow region with a low refractive 
index (known as the slot) positioned between two sections with a high refractive index1. This novel design utilizes 
the discontinuity at the interfaces of these zones to tightly contain and direct light, mostly within the slot. Slot 
waveguides, which were created during the early twentyfirst century, have seen tremendous development and 
are now essential elements in integrated photonic circuits1,2. Their exceptional capacity to confine light within 
relatively small volumes amplifies light-matter interactions, rendering them especially suitable in applications 
that demand high field intensities. Moreover, their ability to be easily included in conventional semiconductor 
manufacturing methods allows for seamless integration with electronic and photonic devices, leading to 
significant progress in optical communications, sensing, and nonlinear optics3–11. Slot waveguides are a significant 
advancement in photonics, providing a combination of excellent performance, small size, and versatile use12–17. 
While their design space may involve only a few geometric parameters (gap, slab width, and slab height), the 
optical response is highly sensitive and nonlinear across these parameters, necessitating careful optimization. 
Recent studies have demonstrated their efficacy in refractive index sensing18, hybrid modulators19–21, nonlinear 
devices22,23, power combiner24 and power splitter25,26 with advancements in fabrication, such as electron-beam 
lithography and reactive ion etching (RIE) supporting sub-100 nm precision. Ongoing research explores novel 
materials, photonic crystal integration, and multi-slot architectures to further improve performance, positioning 
slot waveguides as a foundational component for compact, high-performance photonic circuits18,22.
Accurate modeling and optimization of nanophotonics structures such as waveguides, ring resonators and 
directional couplers generally rely upon numerical methods such as finite difference method27, finite element 
method (FEM)28, block-iterative frequency-domain method29, and plane wave expansion method30,31. However, 
these methods require significant computer resources when dealing with complex photonic device structures, 
which need to be simulated multiple times to obtain an optimized design. Such iterative analysis also depends 
upon the number of input design parameters that need to be optimized. Currently, deep and machine learning 
are showing their promising advantage in many fields, such as image processing32, speech processing33, bio-
medical signal processing34, pattern recognition35, robotics36, and many more. Researchers have also explored 
the application of machine learning in the field of photonics, including multimode fibers37, plasmonic38, 
metamaterials39, biosensing40, meta-surface design41,42, optical communications43 and networking44. 
Kiarashinejad et al.45 proposed a deep learning-based algorithm using dimensionality reduction technique to 
understand the properties of electromagnetic wave-matter interaction in nanostructures. A geometric deep-

Many other studies used ML/transfer learning algorithms like an artificial neural network29, Bayesian neural 
network48, multiple additive regression trees49, support vector machine50, multivariate adaptive regression 
splines51, gradient boosting machine52, k-nearest neighbors53, random forest54, Gaussian process regressions55, 
and boosted regression tree56 for developing learning models in several other fields of research. It has also been 
reported that in a few cases the SVM performed better than multiple linear regression and ANN as SVM does 
not suffer from the problem of local minima, fewer learning parameters to be selected by SVM, and it produces 
stable and reproducible results44. Similar comparative studies for the prediction ability of ML algorithms are 
reported by many36,57,58. It has also been observed that the predictability of the algorithms is largely dependent 
on the data and the predictor selection. So, the current study put an effort into evaluating the three most 
popular ML algorithms to select proficient algorithms to develop a training model for computing various optical 
properties of the slot waveguide structure.
Here, we evaluated three machine learning (ML) algorithms to select a proficient algorithm to develop a 
training model for computing various optical properties of the slot waveguide structure. The trained model can 
help optimize the parameters of the slot waveguide based on the simulated effective refractive index (neff) and 
confinement power (Pconf). We combine finite element simulations and ML approaches for quick and accurate 
computation. This paper aims to design an ML model that can be trained efficiently to estimate the neff and 
Pconf for different geometric parameters of a slot waveguide structure.
Methods
In this work, we have used a slot waveguide to optimize the performance parameters with the help of three 
optimization algorithm techniques. A two-dimensional (2D) view of the slot waveguide with its electric field 
profile is shown in Fig. 1. The slot waveguide consists of two silicon (Si) high-refractive-index (3.47@1.55µm) 
regions separated by a narrow low-refractive-index slot (air), and silicon dioxide (1.45@1.55µm) as substrate. 
The discontinuity in the electric-field displacement field D=ϵE at the interface between materials with different 
permittivities (ϵ) leads to a strong enhancement of the electric field E within the low-permittivity slot. This results 
in a significant portion of the optical mode being confined in the slot region, even though it is of a lower index. 
A 2D finite element method-based approach has been adopted to find the performance parameters effective 
refractive index (neff) and confinement power (Pconf) of the slot waveguide. The performance parameters of 
the slot waveguide have been calculated by changing the geometric parameters, such as the gap between the slot 
(g), slab width (w), and slab height (h). It is essential to prepare proper data sets for the training and testing of 
the proposed ML models. Hence, the data generated from the simulation using COMSOL Multiphysics were 
utilized. In this study, a set of slot waveguide geometric data, including gap, slab width, and slab height, were 
taken as labeled input variables, while the effective refractive index and power confinement were taken as labeled 
output variables, as shown in Fig. 2. The range of the input data set for the gap, slab width, and slab height were 
taken from 10 to 90 nm with an interval of 10 nm, 145 nm to 345 nm with an interval of 5 nm, and 200 nm to 
300 nm with an interval of 10 nm respectively.

Random forest (RF)
RF is an ensemble learning algorithm with an ensemble of decision trees to make predictions in classification as 
well as regression-related problems [41]. In the case of regression-related problems, the algorithm produces the 
class variable as the mean prediction of all decision trees. Bootstrapped training samples are used to build the 
individual trees in RF ensembles. For the improvement of prediction by making it robust to outliers and noise, 
it is ensured that trees are decorrelated by considering a small group of randomly selected preditors at each split 
while growing decision trees53. By growing the forest up to a predefined number of trees, it creates trees that have 
high variance and low bias58. So, finally, the prediction on a test/new data x  can be obtained as62,63:

SVR58, and RF54,58 for their ability to predict neff and Pconf. The above ML algorithms are executed in the 
Weka Version 3.8.3 environment64–66.
While training the ANN model in Weka, the ‘multi-layer perceptron’ package was used with the number

Results and discussion
As discussed in the methodology section, this study evaluated three ML algorithms: ANN, SVR, and RF to 
identify a proficient algorithm for the development of the training model for this study. The algorithms were 
trained for both neff and Pconf separately. Figure 4 shows the observed and predicted neff using all three 
algorithms, and it is evident that RF outperformed the other two with the MAE, RMSE, R2, and NSE values of 
0.007, 0.054, 0.961, and 0.960, respectively. However, the statistical metrics associated with ANN and SVR are 
quite comparable. Further, a similar finding was also observed for Pconf training with RF outperforming the 
ANN and SVR by a significant margin (Fig. 5). The MAE, RMSE, R2, and NSE values were observed to be 0.129, 
0.185, 0.998, and 0.998, respectively. It can also observed that RF has a consistent performance for all ranges of 
neff and Pconf values, whereas ANN and SVR show over and under predictions at different ranges of neff and 
Pconf values. Since in both cases, RF has a superior proficiency in predicting neff and Pconf, this study selected 
RF as the training algorithm for further analysis.
In addition to the superior overall performance of RF for predicting neff and Pconf, this study evaluated the 
range of gap, slab height, and slab width where the trained algorithm performs best among the range of the three 
variables considered in this study. Figure 6 compares the MAE, RMSE, R2, and NSE values at different variable 
values and the superior ranges in the case of both neff and Pconf.
It can be observed that for both neff and Pconf, the model performs best at a gap size of 80 nm and the 
same for the slab height are 290 nm. Whereas, for the slab width, the model has a consistently good prediction 
between 175 and 325 nm in the case of neff. Further, for slab width in Pconf the initial ranges the model had 
poor performance but the performance improved and became consistently good between 175 and 275 nm slab 
width size, and then continued to deteriorate for higher values.
As discussed in previous paragraphs, the RF algorithm has superior proficiency in predicting neff and 
Pconf. However, we have put effort into identifying the best combinations of the input parameters considered 
in this study. The absolute errors calculated in Fig. 7 show that in most of the combinations, the absolute error is 
less than 0.2 nm, whereas there are several regions in the area plot with green shades having values close to zero. 
This signifies that those combinations can be considered while selecting the input values in future investigations. 
Further, it can be observed from Fig. 7a–c that the performance of the model has slightly poorer results in 
the extremely high ranges of gap and slab height, and while finding the best combination of slab width and 
slab height it was observed that the low range of slab height (200 to 205 nm) the performance is low in the 
case of neff. These observations suggested avoiding those ranges of gap, slab height, and slab width in future 
investigations. Similar to neff, the higher ranges of the absolute error are scattered over the different ranges 
of gap, slab height, and slab width for Pconf. This analysis aims to provide guidance of the fresh experimental 
setup and the fabrication. Poor performance of RF at the two extremes suggests that the researchers should not 
consider these ranges of geometric parameters for their fresh experimental setup, targeting the conservation of 
time and resources. Conclusively, depending upon the accuracy requirement a suitable combination of the input 
parameters can be selected.
Next, in Fig. 8a,b, we have compared the actual and predicted neff and Pconf for different trained RF, 
ANN and SVR models at unknown gap and slab height parameters. It should be noted that the generated input 
training dataset did not have any value corresponding to gap = 85 nm and slab height = 295 nm. ANN and SVR 
models were not able to predict the actual pattern (shown by the black solid line) well, and the predicted values 
(shown by red, blue, and green filled circles) steered away from the actual values as slab width increases from 
145 to 345 mm. The residue of the predicted values from the actual values for the RF, ANN, and SVR algorithms

Conclusion
In conclusion, machine learning algorithms have been used to accurately predict the performance parameters 
of the slot waveguide i.e., neff and Pconf. ANN, SVR, and RF algorithms were trained for both neff and Pconf 
separately, and it was observed that RF outperformed the other two with MAE, RMSE, R2 and NSE values of 
0.007, 0.054, 0.961, and 0.960 for neff and 0.129, 0.185, 0.998, and 0.998 for Pconf, respectively. In addition to 
the overall superior performance of RF for predicting neff and Pconf, this study evaluated the range of gap, 
slab height, and slab width where the trained algorithm performs best among the range of the three variables 
considered in this study. It can be observed that for both neff and Pconf the model performs best at a gap size 
of 80 nm and the same for the slab height are 290 nm. However, for the slab width, the model has a consistently 
good prediction between 175 and 325 nm for neff. The prediction accuracy achieved through RF signifies the 
generic nature of the trained model (AMPLslot) and can be highly recommended as a cost and time-effective 
alternative tool to simulation or laboratory trials for experimental design and fabrication. This model can be 
extended to develop a more generalized machine learning model for complex photonics designs, considering 
different materials and other input parameters with the aid of deep neural networks.
